755.t: Eve of the An Lushan Rebellion
755.d: The Tang in the winter of Tianbao 14 (755), before An Lushan's rising. On the frontiers stood ten military governorships and pacification commissions: Anxi, Beiting, Hexi, Longyou, Shuofang, Hedong, Fanyang, Pinglu, Jiannan and the Five Commands of Lingnan; in the interior, investigation commissioners still supervised the prefectures and counties in fifteen circuits. An Lushan alone held the three fanzhen of Fanyang, Pinglu and Hedong, with nearly 200,000 troops. All around, Tibet, Nanzhao, the Uyghurs, Balhae, the Khitans and the Xi lay in wait.

757.d: Spring and summer of Zhide 2 (757): An Lushan was killed by his son An Qingxu in the 1st month, but the Yan army still held the two capitals, Hebei and most of Henan. Emperor Suzong of Tang moved from Lingwu to Fengxiang, while Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan held Suiyang to the death, shielding the Jiang–Huai region. The crack troops of Anxi, Beiting, Hexi and Longyou were sent east against the rebels, and Tibet took the chance to eat into Longyou; Nanzhao took Xizhou.

765.t: Hebei autonomy · Hexi and Longyou lost
765.d: After the An Lushan Rebellion was put down (763), the court divided Hebei among the surrendered rebel generals Li Huaixian, Li Baochen, Tian Chengsi and Xue Song, and Hebei's autonomy took shape; Hou Xiyi and Li Zhengji held Ziqing. Tibet took the chance to seize all of Longyou, broke into Chang'an for a time in Guangde 1 (763) and took Liangzhou in 764; Hexi fell back on Ganzhou, Suzhou, Guazhou and Shazhou, and Anxi and Beiting were cut off from the Central Plains. In the interior military governors and surveillance commissioners were set up everywhere, and fanzhen covered the empire.

784.d: Emperor Dezong set out to curb the fanzhen, and from Jianzhong 2 (781) the Hebei fanzhen joined forces against him; in 782 Zhu Tao, Wang Wujun, Tian Yue and Li Na agreed to proclaim themselves kings (the "Rebellion of the Four Fanzhen"), and Li Xilie of Huaixi called himself Supreme Commander of All Under Heaven, then proclaimed himself emperor at Bianzhou in 784 with the dynastic name Great Chu. In 783 the Jingyuan troops mutinied and set up Zhu Ci, who held Chang'an and proclaimed himself emperor (as Qin, later renamed Han), and Dezong fled to Fengtian; in 784 Li Huaiguang of Shuofang also rebelled and held Hezhong, and Dezong fled again to Liangzhou, which he raised to Xingyuan Fu. In the same year he issued an edict of self-reproach; Wang Wujun, Tian Yue and Li Na gave up their royal titles and submitted, and Li Sheng recovered Chang'an. Tibet had taken all of Hexi except the isolated city of Shazhou.

805.t: Tibet at its height · Fanzhen everywhere
805.d: In the Zhenyuan era Tibet took Shazhou (786), Beiting (790) and Xizhou (792), and the Four Garrisons of Anxi fell one after another; the Tang lost the Western Regions, and the Uyghurs and Tibet fought back and forth over the lands north of the Tian Shan. In 794 Yimouxun of Nanzhao swore a covenant with the Tang on the Diancang Mountains and returned to the Tang against Tibet, and Wei Gao, military governor of Xichuan, routed the Tibetans. In the interior the three Hebei fanzhen, Li Shigu of Ziqing (twelve prefectures) and Wu Shaocheng of Huaixi took power without the court's sanction, and the court tolerated them. In 805 Emperor Shunzong came to the throne and launched the Yongzhen Reform, which soon failed.

820.d: Emperor Xianzong used force to curb the fanzhen: in 806 he put down Liu Pi of Xichuan and Yang Huilin of Xiasui, in 807 Li Qi of Zhexi; in 817 Li Su entered Caizhou on a snowy night and captured Wu Yuanji; in 819 Li Shidao of Ziqing was killed and his lands divided into the three fanzhen of Tianping, Pinglu and Yanhai. Wang Chengzong of Chengde gave up the two prefectures of Dezhou and Dizhou, and Tian Hongzheng of Weibo and Liu Zong of Lulong submitted in turn. "For nearly sixty years since the Guangde era the fanzhen had defied the court in more than thirty prefectures of Henan and Hebei, appointing their own officials and paying no tribute or taxes; now all of them obeyed the court's commands." In the north the Uyghurs and Tibet faced each other north and south of the Tian Shan.

851.t: Zhang Yichao returns to allegiance · Hehuang recovered
851.d: In 840 the Yenisei Kyrgyz sacked the Uyghur khagan's camp and the Uyghur Khaganate collapsed, its people moving west to the Tian Shan and Hexi; in 842 the Tibetan tsenpo Langdarma was assassinated and the empire split apart. The Tang took the chance to recover the three prefectures of Qinzhou, Yuanzhou and Anle Zhou and the Seven Passes in 849; in 848 Zhang Yichao of Shazhou rose and drove out the Tibetans, and in 851 he sent envoys to present the maps and household registers of eleven prefectures to the court. The Tang set up the Guiyi Jun with Zhang Yichao as military governor. In the Huichang era Liu Zhen of Zelu was put down (844), while the three Hebei fanzhen remained hereditary and independent.

881.d: In Qianfu 1–2 (874–875) Wang Xianzhi and then Huang Chao rose; Huang Chao fought his way through the Jiang–Huai region and Lingnan, took Guangzhou in 879, entered Chang'an in the 12th month of 880, and took the throne as emperor with the dynastic name Great Qi. Emperor Xizong fled to Chengdu. Shi Pu of Xuzhou, Qin Zongquan of Caizhou and others set themselves up amid the chaos; Li Keyong and his father of the Shatuo were defeated by a Tang army in 880 and fled north to the Tatars. Zhang Yichao of the Guiyi Jun recovered Liangzhou (861), and Pugu Jun of the Xizhou Uyghurs took Qocho and Beiting (866). Nanzhao repeatedly raided Annan (862–866) and Xichuan (869–870), and its own strength declined too.

895.d: After Huang Chao's defeat and death (884), the Tang court's orders did not reach beyond Guanzhong. Zhu Quanzhong held Bianzhou and swallowed up Henan; Li Keyong held Hedong and Zhaoyi and was his sworn enemy; Li Maozhen held Fengxiang and Shannan West Circuit and joined forces with Wang Xingyu of Binning and Han Jian of Huazhou to hold the court in their grip; Wang Jian took Xichuan, Yang Xingmi held Huainan and Xuanshe, Qian Liu held Hangzhou, Dong Chang proclaimed himself emperor at Yuezhou (the state of Great Yue Luoping), Wang Chao held Fujian, and Ma Yin and Liu Jianfeng took Hunan. Weibo, Chengde and Liu Rengong of Youzhou wavered between Zhu and Li.

907.t: Fall of Tang · Five Dynasties begin
907.d: In the 4th month of Tianyou 4 (907) Zhu Quanzhong usurped the Tang throne, changed his name to Zhu Huang and founded the state of Liang (Later Liang) with its capital at Kaifeng; the Tang came to an end. Li Keyong of Hedong, Li Maozhen of Fengxiang, Wang Jian of Xichuan and Yang Wo of Huainan (Wu) still used the Tang reign title "Tianyou" and opposed Liang; in the 9th month of the same year Wang Jian proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu (Former Shu). Qian Liu was invested as Prince of Wuyue and Ma Yin as Prince of Chu; Wang Shenzhi held Fujian (invested as Prince of Min in 909), Liu Yin held Guangzhou, and Liu Shouguang of Youzhou, Wang Rong of Zhenzhou and Wang Chuzhi of Dingzhou each went their own way. In the same year the Khitan leader Yelü Abaoji took the title of khagan.

926.t: Later Tang unites the north · Khitan destroys Balhae
926.d: Li Cunxu proclaimed himself emperor in 923 (Later Tang), destroyed Liang that same year and in 925 sent Guo Chongtao to destroy Former Shu, briefly uniting the north with Ba and Shu; in 926, in the Xingjiao Gate incident, Emperor Zhuangzong of Later Tang was killed and Li Siyuan took the throne (Emperor Mingzong). Shu was divided between Meng Zhixiang (Xichuan) and Dong Zhang (Dongchuan). Yelü Abaoji of the Khitan proclaimed himself emperor in 916, destroyed Balhae in 926 and turned it into the state of Dongdan; Abaoji died of illness on his way home. In the south Wu, Wuyue, Min, Chu, Southern Han (whose ruler Liu Yan proclaimed himself emperor in 917) and Jingnan stood side by side.

938.t: Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun pass to Khitan
938.d: In 936 Shi Jingtang, military governor of Hedong, colluded with the Khitans and borrowed their troops to destroy Later Tang, calling himself their "son emperor"; he ceded the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun to the Khitans (formally handed over in 938) and paid 300,000 bolts of silk a year. From then on the Central Plains lost the barrier of the Great Wall in the north. In the same period Meng Zhixiang proclaimed himself emperor in 934 and founded Later Shu, Xu Zhigao (Li Bian) replaced Wu with Southern Tang in 937, Duan Siping of the Dali Kingdom destroyed Dayining (937), Wang Geon of Goryeo united the Korean peninsula (936), and in Giao Châu Ngô Quyền crushed Southern Han at the Bạch Đằng River in 938; Vietnam moved toward independence.

947.d: The Later Jin emperor Shi Chonggui (Emperor Chu) called himself the Khitans' grandson but not their subject, which led to war; in 946 Du Chongwei surrendered to the Khitans with an army of 100,000 at the Zhongdu Bridge, and in the 1st month of 947 Yelü Deguang entered Kaifeng and Later Jin fell; in the 2nd month he changed the dynastic name to Great Liao. Liao troops went out in all directions plundering for supplies ("gathering grass and grain"), resistance broke out across the Central Plains, and in the 3rd month Yelü Deguang went back north; he died on the way in the 4th month. Liu Zhiyuan, military governor of Hedong, proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan in the 2nd month (Later Han) and entered Kaifeng in the 6th month. In the south, Southern Tang destroyed Min in 945, Li Renda of Fuzhou went over to Wuyue, and the three prefectures of Qinzhou, Chengzhou and Jiezhou surrendered to Later Shu.

951.t: Later Zhou founded · Southern Tang conquers Chu
951.d: In 950 Emperor Yin of Later Han murdered his senior ministers; Guo Wei rose at Yedu and entered Kaifeng, and in the 1st month of 951 proclaimed himself emperor and founded Later Zhou. Liu Zhiyuan's younger brother Liu Chong proclaimed himself emperor at Taiyuan (Northern Han) and became a dependent of Liao. In the south the Ma brothers of Chu fell out, and in 951 Southern Tang took the chance to destroy Chu; Southern Han seized Chu's prefectures in Lingnan along with Chenzhou and Lianzhou; Liu Congxiao of Quanzhou held the two prefectures of Quanzhou and Zhangzhou (the Qingyuan Jun). Later Shu had already gained the four prefectures of Qinzhou, Fengzhou, Chengzhou and Jiezhou.

959.t: Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou campaigns south and north
959.d: Emperor Shizong of Later Zhou, Chai Rong, reorganized the army and crushed Northern Han and Liao at the Battle of Gaoping in 954; in 955 he took the four prefectures of Qinzhou, Fengzhou, Chengzhou and Jiezhou from Later Shu in the west; in 956–958 he campaigned three times against Southern Tang, which ceded its fourteen prefectures north of the Yangtze (Yangzhou, Taizhou, Chuzhou, Hezhou, Shouzhou, Haozhou, Sizhou, Chuzhou, Guangzhou, Haizhou, Shuzhou, Qizhou, Huangzhou and Luzhou), accepted the Yangtze as the border and gave up the title of emperor for "ruler of the state". In 959 he campaigned north against Liao and in forty-two days recovered the two prefectures of Yingzhou and Mozhou and the three passes of Waqiao, Yijin and Yukou, but soon died of illness. Hunan was by then held by Zhou Xingfeng (the Wuping Jun).

965.t: Northern Song founded · South first, then north
965.d: In 960 Zhao Kuangyin replaced Zhou with Song in the Chenqiao mutiny, with Kaifeng as his capital. He adopted the strategy of "south first, then north": in 963, asking for passage through Jingnan, he took both Jingnan under the Gao family and Hunan under the Zhou family at one stroke; in the winter of 964 Wang Quanbin attacked Shu, Meng Chang surrendered in the 1st month of 965, and Later Shu fell. Southern Tang and Wuyue followed the Song calendar, while Northern Han still relied on Liao. Quanzhou and Zhangzhou passed to Chen Hongjin (the Pinghai Jun). In Giao Châu the Ngô dynasty was in decline and about to break up among the "Twelve Warlords".

975.t: Song conquers Southern Han and Southern Tang
975.d: In 971 Pan Mei took Guangzhou and Liu Chang of Southern Han surrendered; in 974 the Song army crossed the Yangtze on a pontoon bridge at Caishi, and in the 11th month of 975 it took Jinling, and Li Yu, the last ruler of Southern Tang, surrendered. In Giao Châu Đinh Bộ Lĩnh put down the Twelve Warlords in 968 and founded the state of Đại Cồ Việt, with its capital at Hoa Lư. By now only Wuyue and the Chen family of Quanzhou and Zhangzhou remained in the south, and Northern Han and Liao in the north.

979.t: Song conquers Northern Han · Battle of the Gaoliang River
979.d: In 978 Chen Hongjin handed over Quanzhou and Zhangzhou, and Qian Chu, King of Wuyue, "surrendered his lands to the Song"; in 979 Emperor Taizong of Song led a campaign against Taiyuan in person, Liu Jiyuan of Northern Han surrendered, and the division of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms came to an end. Taizong pressed on to attack Liao, hoping to take Yan and Yun, but in the 7th month was badly beaten at the Gaoliang River outside Youzhou; the Song never recovered the Sixteen Prefectures of Yan and Yun. In the northwest the Tangut Dingnan Jun, the Guiyi Jun and the Ganzhou Uyghur Kingdom in Hexi, the Kingdom of Qocho (Uyghurs), the Kingdom of Khotan and the Kara-Khanid Khanate in the Western Regions, and in the southwest the Dali Kingdom and the Tibetan tribes, all lay outside the Song borders.
